# Āneñjasappāya Sutta (MN 106 (PTS MN ii 261))

**ID:** MN 106 (PTS MN ii 261)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Āneñjasappāya Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Conducive to the Imperturbable
**PTS:** MN ii 261
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Āneñjasappāya Sutta* ("Conducive to the Imperturbable", MN 106 / PTS MN ii 261) is a discourse in the Majjhimanikāya outlining progressive paths toward meditative absorption, the formless attainments, and final liberation [Rogell 2003]. Opening with the admonition that sensual pleasures are impermanent, hollow, and deceptive (*māyākatam*) [Westerhoff 2018], the Buddha details how practitioners can transcend the disturbances of sensuality and material forms by cultivating the "imperturbable" (*āneñja*), a state associated with the fourth *jhāna* and higher meditative states [Pande 1974; Rogell 2003; Polak 2011]. The discourse presents specific reflective approaches leading to the dimension of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), including the contemplation that the cessation of perceptions is peaceful, the insight into selflessness, and the reflection that one does not belong to anything [Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation; Thanissaro 2013]. A central doctrinal emphasis of the sutta is that subtle equanimity (*upekkhā*) reached at these refined levels must not become an object of attachment; clinging must be relinquished through reflections such as "what exists, what has become, that I abandon" (*yad atthi, yaṁ bhūtaṁ taṁ pajahāmi*) so that consciousness becomes unestablished (*apatiṭṭhita*) and achieves complete liberation [Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation; Thanissaro 2013]. Grzegorz Polak notes that the sutta contains a distinctive meditative schema wherein the higher formless dimensions are preceded directly by *āneñja* rather than the standard fourfold formless sequence [Polak 2011].

A full parallel to the sutta is found in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 75), and the text is cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 19.2).

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: MA 75 淨不動道
- Mentioned in: Kv 19.2 Suññatākathā

**Sources**

- [Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation] Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation: Excursions into the Thought-world of the Pali Discourses (1) — Analysis of the three approaches to the base of nothingness, abandonment of clinging to equanimity, and unestablished consciousness.
- [Westerhoff 2018] Jan Westerhoff, The Golden Age of Indian Buddhist Philosophy in the First Millennium CE (2018) — Quotation of the opening passage on the illusory and deceptive nature of sensual desires.
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner’s Study Guide (Majjhima Nikāya) (2003) — Overview of the discourse's meditative scheme and warning against clinging to higher states.
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhāna: Towards a Critical Reconstruction of Early Buddhist Soteriology (2011) — Analysis of the unique meditation scheme and structural relationship between āneñja and the formless attainments.
- [Pande 1974] Govind Chandra Pande, Studies in the Origins of Buddhism (1974) — Note on the series of imperturbable states described in the sutta.
- [Thanissaro 2013] Thanissaro Bhikkhu, The Truth of Rebirth And Why it Matters for Buddhist Practice (2013) — Discussion of not-self contemplation leading to the dimension of nothingness and the danger of subtle clinging to equanimity.
